subtitle: Turn what navigators see into fixes in forms, letters and processes, test changes in small steps, measure results honestly and share the work and the credit with the communities involved.
audience: For program managers, policy staff and leaders who can change processes, forms and letters. It complements the app's equity analysis tools and does not replace formal policy review, legal review or required equity analysis.

lessons.title: What navigators see that the system does not
objectives: Explain why navigators notice patterns that agency data often misses.
Describe feeding back as a core part of navigation, not an extra.
Set up a simple way to collect what navigators see without identifying people.
Respond to a navigator's report of a pattern in a way that encourages more.
lessons.teaching:
Navigators see the system from the family's side of the table. They notice which letter confuses people, which step makes families give up and which phrase lands badly in their community. Agency data often shows that something went wrong, such as a missed renewal, but not why. Navigators often know why.

Feeding back is part of the job. California's Department of Social Services describes child welfare cultural brokers as also working to change systems to reduce disproportionality and disparities. In this pathway, feeding back means telling the agency where a process keeps breaking down for a community, so it can be fixed for the next family.

Make it easy and safe. A short shared log, or a standing agenda item, where navigators can note a pattern without naming anyone, works better than hoping problems surface on their own. Ask for three things: what happened, how often it seems to happen and which step or document was involved. Keep personal details out. The point is the pattern, not the person.

How you respond matters most. If a navigator reports a confusing letter and nothing happens, they will stop reporting. Thank them, say what you will do with it and tell them later what came of it, even when the answer is "not yet." A navigator who sees a fix happen will keep watching for the next one.
lessons.keyPoint: Navigators see why things go wrong. Give them a simple, safe way to report patterns, and always tell them what happened next.
lessons.example: Practice case: The navigator tells the program manager that five families in the past month misunderstood the same renewal letter and thought their services were ending.
lessons.question: What should the program manager do?
choices: Explain that the letter follows required wording and cannot be changed.
Thank the navigator, ask which parts confused families, log the pattern and set a date to report back on what can change.
Ask the navigator to explain the letter to every family from now on.
feedback: Some wording may be required, but the parts around it often are not. Closing the door teaches the navigator not to report again.
This values the report, gathers the detail needed to act and commits to closing the loop.
This helps families now but makes the navigator a permanent patch for a fixable problem.
lessons.reflection: When someone outside your team tells you a process is not working, what usually happens next? What would you want to happen?
lessons.action: Set up a simple way, such as a shared log or a standing agenda item, for navigators or front-line staff to report patterns without naming people.

check.question: What should a navigator's pattern report include?
check.correct: What happened, how often it seems to happen and which step or document was involved, without identifying people.
wrong: The names and case numbers of every family affected.
Only problems the navigator can personally fix.
check.feedback: The goal is the pattern, not the person. Leaving out personal details protects families and keeps attention on the step that needs fixing.

lessons.title: From a story to a fix
objectives: Check a navigator's report against the program's own information.
Find the part of a form, letter or process that can change.
Test a change in a small step before rolling it out, using a Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle.
Involve the people affected in designing and testing the fix.
lessons.teaching:
A pattern a navigator reports is a strong lead. Check it against what the program already knows. How many renewals lapse after that letter goes out? Do some communities miss the step more than others? You may not have perfect data, and that is fine. The goal is to understand the problem well enough to try a fix.

Then find what can change. Required legal wording may have to stay, but the explanation around it, the order of information, the headings, the plain-language summary on top and the translated versions often can change. Processes have the same kind of room: when a call happens, who makes it, how many reminders go out and in what language.

Test small. The Institute for Healthcare Improvement describes the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle as a way to test a change: plan the test, try it, study the results and decide what to change next. A new letter can be tried with ten families before it goes to ten thousand. Navigators are ideal partners here, because they can tell you quickly whether families understood it.

Involve the people affected. Ask a few families, through the navigator and with their agreement, to read a draft and say what they think it means. Their answers will tell you more than any internal review. A fix designed with the community is more likely to work, and more likely to be trusted.
lessons.keyPoint: Check the pattern, find what can change, test it small and test it with the people it is for.
lessons.example: Practice case: The program manager and the newer colleague are deciding how to fix the confusing renewal letter. The newer colleague suggests rewriting every letter the program sends, all at once.
lessons.question: What should the program manager suggest?
choices: Rewrite everything at once, since the letters are clearly a problem.
Leave the letters as they are and add a phone number for questions.
Start with the one renewal letter, add a plain-language summary at the top, test it with a small group of families through the navigator and adjust before sending it widely.
feedback: Ambitious, but a large rewrite with no testing may create new confusion and takes much longer to finish.
A phone number may help some families, but it leaves the confusing letter in place and adds calls for staff.
This fixes the known problem first, tests it with the people it is for and builds evidence for the next change.
lessons.reflection: Think of a form or letter your program uses. If a family misread it, which part would they most likely misread?
lessons.action: Choose one confusing letter or form. Write a three-sentence plain-language summary for the top, and plan how you would test it with a few families.

check.question: What is a Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle?
check.correct: A way to test a change: plan the test, try it, study the results and decide what to change next.
wrong: A way to approve a change before anyone tries it.
A one-time survey sent after a change is made.
check.feedback: The Institute for Healthcare Improvement describes PDSA as a cycle for testing changes, usually several times, learning from each test before spreading the change.

lessons.title: Measuring results honestly
objectives: Choose measures tied to the step the navigator or the fix is meant to change.
Tell the difference between strong evidence and program-reported results.
Report results with their limits, without overstating what they show.
Measure processes and outcomes, never individual people's culture or worth.
lessons.teaching:
Measure what the change was meant to change. If a navigator is attached to assessments, watch how many assessments happen on the first scheduled date. If a letter was rewritten, watch whether renewals are completed on time. Measures tied to a specific step are easier to collect and easier to believe than broad measures like "better outcomes."

Know the strength of your evidence. The 2021 autism family navigation trial was randomized: families were assigned by chance to navigation or usual care, so the difference between groups is strong evidence. Many navigator programs report their own results instead. The Sacramento Observer reported in 2025 that, of 499 families served by Sacramento County's Cultural Broker program, 96% had their emergency referrals closed without child welfare court intervention, a figure given by the county staff member who manages the program. That is useful, but it is program-reported and has no comparison group, so it cannot show how much of the result the brokers caused.

Report your own results the same way. Say what you measured, over what time, compared with what, and what else changed at the same time. Leaders are often tempted to round a promising number into a proven one. Resist it. Overstated results are hard to walk back, and they can cost a program its credibility when the next number is less dramatic.

Measure processes and outcomes, not people. Do not score a person's culture, rate a community's "compliance" or treat course completion as proof that a team has changed. The question is whether the system works better for the people it serves.
lessons.keyPoint: Measure the step you meant to change, know whether your evidence is strong or program-reported and report results with their limits.
lessons.example: Practice case: A senior leader wants to announce that a pilot navigator program "cut missed assessments by 60%." The supervisor knows the figure compares six months before the pilot with six months after, during which the assessment scheduling system also changed.
lessons.question: What should the supervisor recommend?
choices: Report that missed assessments fell 60% in the six months after the pilot began, note that scheduling also changed and describe what further measurement would show more.
Announce the 60% figure, since it is accurate.
Say nothing until a full randomized trial is done.
feedback: This shares a promising result honestly, names what else could explain it and points to how to learn more.
The number is accurate but the claim is not. Another change happened at the same time, so the drop cannot be credited to navigators alone.
Waiting for a trial may hide useful information. Honest reporting of a promising result is better than silence.
lessons.reflection: When you have seen a striking number about a program, what questions did you want answered before you believed it?
lessons.action: Pick one measure tied to a specific step in your program. Write down how you would collect it and what else could change it besides your fix.

check.question: Why are program-reported results weaker evidence than a randomized trial?
check.correct: Without a comparison group assigned by chance, other changes or differences could explain the result.
wrong: Because programs always report false numbers.
Because results from social services do not count as evidence.
check.feedback: Program-reported results can be accurate and useful. Without a fair comparison, though, they cannot show how much of the change the program caused.

lessons.title: Sharing the work and the credit
objectives: Involve navigators and communities in deciding which problems to fix first.
Credit navigators and communities for the changes they helped make.
Close the loop publicly when a fix is made.
Connect navigator feedback to the program's equity analysis and policy review.
lessons.teaching:
System change works better when the people affected help decide what to change. Ask navigators and community partners which problems matter most to the families they serve. Their list may differ from yours, and that difference is worth knowing.

Give credit where it is due. When a letter is rewritten because a navigator noticed the problem, say so, in team meetings, in reports and to the community organization the navigator works for. Credit is not a courtesy. It shows communities that their knowledge changes things, and it makes the next report more likely.

Close the loop publicly. Tell the navigators and, where appropriate, the community what changed and why. If something could not change, say that too, and say why. People can accept "we could not change the required wording, but we added a plain summary" much more easily than silence.

Connect this work to the program's formal tools. The app's equity analysis courses and tools help programs look at who a policy or process affects and how. What navigators see is exactly the kind of information those analyses need. Bring navigator patterns into equity analyses, budget conversations and policy reviews, so they shape decisions before problems reach families, not only after.
lessons.keyPoint: Let communities help choose what to fix, credit the people who found the problem and close the loop publicly. Bring what navigators see into formal reviews.
lessons.example: Practice case: A process change based on navigator feedback is finished. The program manager's draft announcement describes it as a staff initiative and does not mention the navigators or the community organization.
lessons.question: What should the supervisor suggest?
choices: Leave it as is. The staff did the work of making the change.
Credit the navigators and their organization for identifying the problem, describe what changed and send the announcement to them too.
Skip the announcement, since it is a small change.
feedback: Staff made the change, but leaving out who found the problem tells communities their knowledge was not valued.
This gives fair credit, closes the loop and makes it more likely that navigators keep reporting problems.
Small changes are worth announcing. Closing the loop is what keeps the feedback coming.
lessons.reflection: Who outside your team has helped improve your work? Did they hear about the difference they made?
lessons.action: Find one change your program made because of feedback from a navigator, partner or family. Make sure the people who raised it know what happened.

check.question: Why credit navigators for changes their feedback produced?
check.correct: It shows communities their knowledge changes things, and it makes future feedback more likely.
wrong: Because navigators are responsible for the change once it is made.
Because credit is required by law.
check.feedback: Staff remain responsible for the change. Credit recognizes where the knowledge came from and keeps the feedback loop alive.

aid.heading: Collect
items: Give navigators a simple, safe way to report patterns.
Ask what happened, how often and which step or document.
Thank them and say what you will do next.

aid.heading: Fix
items: Check the pattern against program information.
Find the parts that can change.
Test small with a Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle.
Test drafts with families, through the navigator and with their agreement.

items: Measure the step you meant to change.
Say what you compared with and over what time.
Name what else changed at the same time.

Close the loop publicly, including what could not change.
Bring navigator patterns into equity analysis and policy review.

sources.title: California Department of Social Services — Cultural Broker Resources

sources.title: Institute for Healthcare Improvement — Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) Worksheet
sources.note: Describes the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle as an essential part of the Model for Improvement for testing a change, and the worksheet as a tool for documenting each test.

sources.title: Feinberg and others — Effect of Family Navigation on Diagnostic Ascertainment Among Children at Risk for Autism: A Randomized Clinical Trial From DBPNet, JAMA Pediatrics (2021)
sources.note: Randomized trial of family navigation for children at risk for autism; families were assigned by chance, and the effect varied by ethnicity and site.

sources.title: The Sacramento Observer — Sacramento County's Cultural Broker program and the decrease in child foster care (April 2025)
sources.note: Reports that Sacramento County's Cultural Broker program began in 2017 and that, of 499 families served, 96% had emergency referrals closed without child welfare court intervention, as stated by the county staff member who manages the program. Program-reported, with no comparison group.

sources.title: Yali Pang and Dana V. Yarbrough — The Promising Practice of Cultural Brokering Support with Culturally Diverse Families of Children with Developmental Disabilities, Developmental Disabilities Network Journal (2023)
sources.note: Recommends that providers work closely with families to decide how cultural brokering support is offered.
